pages.text: There are five species that earn the name big cat: the lion, the tiger, the leopard, the jaguar, and the snow leopard. Four of the five can roar: a sound produced by a specially adapted larynx that no other cat family member can replicate. The snow leopard, the exception, cannot produce a true roar, though it makes a range of deep, powerful calls of its own. A lion's roar can be heard eight kilometres away on a still night. A tiger's roar can stun prey at close range.

image.note: Illustration: the five big cats shown to scale against a human silhouette

pages.text: Big cats are the apex predators of their ecosystems. They sit at the top of the food chain: nothing hunts them, and everything beneath them is shaped by their presence. When big cats are removed from an ecosystem, populations of prey animals explode, vegetation is overgrazed, and the entire system shifts. This is why ecologists call them keystone species.

All five big cats are threatened. The tiger is the most endangered of the five. The snow leopard, the jaguar, and the lion are all classified as vulnerable or endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. The leopard is the most adaptable and the most widespread, but its numbers too are declining across most of its range. The twentieth century was catastrophic for big cats, and the twenty-first offers only cautious hope.

A big cat's body is a hunting instrument tuned over millions of years. Forward-facing eyes judge distance for the killing leap. A tapetum, a mirror behind the retina, doubles the light reaching it, giving night vision far beyond ours. Whiskers map the dark. Retractable claws stay razor sharp because they never touch the ground until they are needed. Even the rough tongue has a purpose: it strips meat from bone and grooms fur to a scentless clean.

The lion is the only big cat that lives in social groups, called prides. A pride typically consists of several related females and their cubs, and one or more males. The females are the primary hunters. The males, with their impressive manes, defend the pride's territory and protect the cubs from rival males.

image.note: Illustration of a pride: two females with cubs resting in shade, male visible at edge of scene

pages.text: Lions hunt cooperatively. Working together, females can bring down prey much larger than any individual lion could manage alone: buffalo, zebra, wildebeest, and even young elephants and hippos. They hunt mostly at night and at dawn, when their superior night vision gives them an advantage over prey that relies more on daylight.

Nigeria's West African lions are genetically distinct from the lions of East and Southern Africa and are critically endangered. The global population of West African lions may be fewer than 400. Yankari National Park in Bauchi State is home to one of the few remaining populations. Protecting it is one of Nigeria's most important conservation responsibilities.

The cheetah breaks the big-cat rules and is not, technically, one of the five. It cannot roar, and its claws do not fully retract, giving it running spikes. In exchange it became the fastest land animal on earth, reaching a hundred kilometres an hour in a few strides. That speed has a cost: a sprinting cheetah overheats within seconds and must stop, and it is so lightly built that other predators steal its kills. Cheetahs once ranged across northern Nigeria and are now gone from the country.

Big cats speak constantly, mostly in ways we miss. A lion's roar is a territorial notice board, readable from kilometres away. Scent marks on bushes carry messages about who passed, when, and whether they were ready to mate. Leopards saw the air with a rasping call. Cubs and mothers keep contact with soft chirps and grunts. To walk through big-cat country is to walk through a landscape saturated with conversation in a language we are only beginning to translate.

The leopard is the most adaptable of the big cats. It can survive in rainforest, savannah, mountains, and even on the edges of cities. It is the strongest climber of the big cats and habitually carries its prey into trees to protect it from lions and hyenas. Its spotted coat, called a rosette pattern, varies significantly between individuals and between regions.

Leopards are found in Nigeria, though they are rarely seen. They are nocturnal, solitary, and extremely secretive. The best evidence of their presence in an area is often pugmarks in mud, scratch marks on trees, or the carcass of prey that has been hoisted into a tree: all signs that a leopard has been there, even if no one saw it.

pages.text: The jaguar, the largest cat in the Americas, is the closest relative of the leopard. The two species evolved from a common ancestor when the ancestors of today's jaguars crossed from Asia into the Americas. Their superficial similarity, both heavily spotted, both powerful climbers and swimmers, reflects a shared evolutionary heritage. Their rosette patterns differ: jaguar rosettes have spots inside them; leopard rosettes do not.

The tiger is the largest cat in the world and one of the most endangered. There are fewer than 4,000 tigers remaining in the wild, confined to fragmented forest patches across Asia. The Siberian tiger, the largest subspecies, lives in the Russian Far East. The Bengal tiger, the most numerous, lives in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, and Bhutan. All subspecies face intense pressure from habitat loss and poaching.

The snow leopard lives where almost nothing else large survives: the high mountains of Central Asia, up to five thousand metres. A tail nearly as long as its body wraps around it like a scarf against the cold and balances it on cliffs. Its pale, blurred coat vanishes against rock and snow so completely that researchers call it the grey ghost. It cannot roar, but it can leap the length of a school classroom in a single bound.

Conservation sometimes works, and the tiger proves it. After a century of catastrophic decline, several countries have begun to reverse it. India, home to most of the world's wild tigers, has seen numbers climb through strict reserves, dedicated patrols, and the relocation of villages away from core habitat. Nepal has done the same. The recovery is fragile and incomplete, but it demolishes the excuse that decline is inevitable. Where people decide big cats will live, they can.

Conflict between big cats and human communities is the central challenge of big cat conservation. As human populations expand and wild habitats shrink, big cats increasingly come into contact with farming and herding communities. Livestock killed by leopards or lions can represent a devastating economic loss for a family with few resources.

The response to this conflict has historically been to kill the cat responsible. This reduces the immediate economic loss but makes the long-term problem worse: removing a cat from a territory often leads to increased conflict as younger, less experienced cats move in and make less efficient hunters.

More effective approaches include compensation schemes that pay farmers for livestock killed by big cats, predator-proof enclosures for livestock, and community benefit programmes that give local people a financial stake in the survival of big cats through wildlife tourism. These approaches require sustained funding and community trust, which are difficult to build and easy to lose.

pages.text: For a child in Nigeria, the lion and the leopard are not distant animals. They share the country. Their survival depends on decisions made by Nigerian communities, Nigerian government, and Nigerian conservationists. The era in which big cats could simply be left to manage themselves in whatever land remained is over. Their future is in human hands.

Nigeria's own big-cat story is not yet finished. Lions cling on in Yankari and Kainji Lake National Parks; leopards survive, unseen, in scattered forests and hills. Camera traps occasionally capture proof that a cat still walks a place everyone assumed was empty. Protecting them means funding rangers, compensating farmers, and refusing the trade in skins and parts. The lion appears on Nigeria's coat of arms. Keeping it on the land, and not only on the emblem, is a choice this generation still has time to make.
